title: KNIGHTMARE
reviewNotes: Begin after ...Kxa1 removes the rook from the earlier eight-piece setup. Reconstructed king approach, two queen-promotion mates, knight-underpromotion mate, and losing repetition of the queen plan. Four branches and every intermediate checked; original sacrifice outside exact scope.
transcript: white sacrifices the knight. Because of course, if the knight is taken, we can just take here with check, and this is completely crushing. So, actually black, instead of taking the knight, has to play king to b2, defend the pawn, and attack the rook. And unfortunately, if white moves now the rook, black can just promote the pawn to a new queen. Black has to give up the rook for it. And from here, two knights will not be enough to checkmate this king. But white is not that naive, and instead of moving the rook away, he plays the brilliant knight f4, leaving the rook to hang a completely, which doesn't seem to make any sense, but it suddenly does after we see that once the king takes the rook, we have knight to d3, and this completely [music] seals the king on the edge of the board, which means that black can only push this pawn, and so he does that. And don't get me wrong, this is still very complicated because the pawn is only four steps away from getting a new queen, and the two knights cannot force a checkmate in any way. But what white did bought himself enough time to start bringing the king. The pawn pushes, and the king walks, and eventually we land in this position, where after pawn to b2, black is only one step away from promoting, and actually winning this game. But this was all part of the plan. Knight to b3 check forces king to be one, and now white plays [music] king to d1, allowing black to promote.
